title: To Err Is Human; To Annotate, SILICON? Reducing Measurement Error in LLM Annotation
description: Decomposes measurement error in LLM-based text annotation into four sources including guideline-induced error and inconsistent annotation behavior, with strategies to minimize error.
content:
1

Cheng, Mayya, and Sedoc

Reducing Measurement Error in LLM Annotation

To Err Is Human; To Annotate, SILICON?

Reducing Measurement Error in LLM Annotation

Xiang Cheng
\AFFRobert H. Smith School of Business, University of Maryland

xccheng@umd.edu \AUTHORRaveesh Mayya, João Sedoc
\AFFLeonard N. Stern School of Business, New York University

{raveesh, jsedoc}@stern.nyu.edu

Updated: 16 October 2025.

(For the Latest Version: Click Here)

ABSTRACT

Unstructured text data annotation is foundational to management research and Large Language Models (LLMs) promise a cost-effective and scalable alternative to human annotation. The validity of insights drawn from LLM annotated data critically depends on minimizing the discrepancy between LLM assigned labels and the unobserved ground truth, as well as ensuring long-term reproducibility of results. This study addresses the gap in the literature on LLM annotation by decomposing measurement error in LLM-based text annotation into four distinct sources: (1) guideline-induced error from inconsistent annotation criteria, (2) baseline-induced error from unreliable human reference standards, (3) prompt-induced error from suboptimal meta-instruction formatting, and (4) model-induced error from architectural differences across LLMs. We develop the SILICON methodology (Systematic Inference with LLMs for Information Classification and Notation) to systematically reduce measurement error from LLM annotation in all four sources above. Empirical validation across seven management research cases shows iteratively refined guidelines substantially increases the LLM-human agreement compared to one-shot guidelines; expert-generated baselines exhibit higher inter-annotator agreement as well as are less prone to producing misleading LLM-human agreement estimates compared to crowdsourced baselines; placing content in the system prompt reduces prompt-induced error; and model performance varies substantially across tasks. To further reduce error, we introduce a cost-effective multi-LLM labeling method, where only low-confidence items receive additional labels from alternative models. Finally, in addressing closed source model retirement cycles, we introduce an intuitive regression-based methodology to establish robust reproducibility protocols. Our evidence indicates that reducing each error source is necessary, and that SILICON supports reproducible, rigorous annotation in management research. An open-source toolkit to operationalize SILICON would be released upon publication.

Large Language Models, Measurement Error, Annotation, Robust Reproducibility

## 1 Introduction

Annotation of unstructured text data, using either crowdsourcing or natural language processing (NLP) tools, is an integral part of management research (Ghose and Ipeirotis 2011, Humphreys and Wang 2018, Loughran and Mcdonald 2014). Machine learning and NLP have been widely employed to extract insights from unstructured text data, helping explain underlying mechanisms such as sentiment and emotional content analysis (Chakraborty et al. 2022, Liu et al. 2019, Melumad et al. 2019, Oh et al. 2023, Yang et al. 2019), product attribute classification (Banerjee et al. 2021, Kwark et al. 2021), advertisement analysis (Lee et al. 2018, Shi et al. 2022), managerial response analysis (Deng and Ravichandran 2023), consumer review analysis (Hong et al. 2021, Mayya et al. 2021), and product categorization (Lee and Hosanagar 2021).

Yet annotation errors can fundamentally distort research conclusions and business decisions. Consider how Saha et al. (2023) found that fear speech is subtle and often appears non-toxic to automated toxicity or hate-speech systems, which can slip past platform moderation. Sap et al. (2019) revealed that toxicity detection systems are twice as likely to incorrectly flag communications from racial minorities as offensive, creating systematic bias in organizational text processing.111These errors extend beyond research settings: in 2023, multiple universities reported cases where “AI-detection” classifiers incorrectly flagged legitimate student work as AI-generated, resulting in false academic misconduct accusations. For instance: see https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/chatgpt-ai-plagiarism-texas-a-and-m-b2341238.html. Given how annotation errors can have severe real-world consequences, minimizing measurement error is therefore the most critical requirement for any annotation workflow.

Large Language Models (LLMs) promise to revolutionize text data annotation with their time-efficiency and cost-effectiveness compared to human annotators. Naturally, researchers are rapidly exploring LLMs for text annotation tasks (Huang et al. 2024, Pangakis et al. 2023, Yeverechyahu et al. 2024, Zhang et al. 2024). Organizations are rapidly adopting LLMs for annotation tasks, with studies showing ChatGPT can match or exceed crowdsourced worker performance in certain contexts (Gilardi et al. 2023). However, this rapid adoption has proceeded without systematic approaches to minimize measurement error, which is the discrepancy between assigned labels and unobserved ground truth. The quality of text annotation processes fundamentally depends on how closely assigned labels align with this ground truth (Yang et al. 2018), yet extant LLM tagging pipelines overlook multiple sources of error that can compound to produce misleading results.

Despite growing interest in adopting LLMs for text annotation tasks (Tan et al. 2024), existing studies seldom identify and fix the distinct sources of measurement error. Extant work validates LLM outputs against human-generated labels (Pangakis et al. 2023) and offers general implementation guidelines (Törnberg 2024), but these efforts examine isolated components of the annotation process rather than decomposing measurement error systematically. Even structured approaches like de Kok (2025) overlook how to systematically assess model confidence for determining when multiple labels are needed (Ipeirotis et al. 2014), and fail to address robust reproducibility concerns as proprietary models face retirement cycles. These gaps limit the development of annotation pipelines that maintain both quality and long-term scientific validity.

We address this critical gap by first formalizing an analytical decomposition of measurement error in LLM annotation. Specifically, measurement error is partitioned into four sources: (1) guideline-induced error from inconsistent annotation criteria, (2) baseline-induced error from unreliable human reference standards, (3) prompt-induced error from suboptimal meta-instruction formatting, and (4) model-induced error from architectural differences across LLMs. We then propose SILICON methodology (Systematic Inference with LLMs for Information Classification and Notation), as illustrated in Figure 1, which provides intervention strategies for each source of error. Furthermore, motivated by the observation that human annotation benefits from multiple labels (Ipeirotis et al. 2014), we present a cost-effective methodology of multi-LLM labeling, where only the low-confidence items receive additional labels using different models. Finally, we introduce regression-based statistical equivalence test to ensure robust reproducibility across multiple LLMs.

To empirically evaluate the effectiveness of SILICON workflow in reducing measurement error, we test multiple state-of-the-art LLMs across seven cases that are representative in management research. These include binary classification, multi-label classification, and multi-class classification tasks. Topic-wise, the tasks include business proposal evaluation (Obermeier and Mayya 2024), review attribute detection (Liu et al. 2019), intent classification and breakdown analysis from customer support dialogs, affective content evaluation (Cheng et al. 2024), language toxicity detection (Saha et al. 2023), criticism stance detection (Peng et al. 2022), and sentiment analysis (Sen et al. 2020).

Our empirical analysis quantifies measurement error reduction across all four sources. Iteratively refined guidelines reduce measurement error by 0.1–0.5 agreement level (measured by Cohen’s Kappa between LLM and human baselines) compared to one-shot guidelines across six tasks for which we developed the guidelines. Expert-generated baselines exhibit 0.1–0.4 higher inter-annotator agreement than crowdsourced baselines, indicating higher reliability of expert baselines. System prompt placement generally reduces prompt-induced error relative to user prompt placement. Model performance varies substantially across tasks and no single model dominating all contexts, necessitating task-specific selection to minimize model-induced error.

In assessing model performance, we also address model confidence and robust reproducibility concerns. Using First-Second Distance metrics, we demonstrate a cost-effective approach to determine confidence thresholds for triggering multiple label generation, with optimal thresholds varying by model type and task complexity. For robust reproducibility, our regression-based statistical equivalence tests reveal that high-performing open-parameter models (e.g., GPT-OSS-120B) can substitute for proprietary models (e.g., GPT-4o) in most tasks, enabling long-term research sustainability despite model retirement cycles from frontier model providers.

Our work contributes to management research methodology by providing the first systematic decomposition and quantification of measurement‐error sources in LLM annotation. Whereas existing approaches focus primarily on isolated performance benchmarking, SILICON embeds error‐minimization at every stage while addressing two critical gaps: determining when model confidence warrants multiple labels and ensuring long-term reproducibility despite model retirement cycles. We introduce a cost-effective approach using First-Second Distance metrics to empirically calibrate confidence thresholds for triggering additional model votes, and develop regression-based statistical equivalence testing to identify open-parameter models that can substitute for proprietary ones. Practically, SILICON offers a parsimonious yet cost-effective approach to LLM annotation. By evaluating model performance and measurement error on representative samples rather than entire datasets, researchers can achieve statistical validity with relatively modest sample sizes (typically 100-200 documents). These findings remain applicable as LLM capabilities evolve because they address fundamental sources of measurement error rather than model-specific implementations. Finally, we will release an open-source toolkit that implements SILICON for practice and research.

## 2 Conceptual Background and Related Literature

### 2.1 Science of Annotation: Prescriptive Annotation Process and Reproducibility

The effectiveness of text annotation processes fundamentally depends on establishing consistent interpretation across annotators, thereby minimizing measurement error that stems from heterogeneous mental models. Many annotation tasks face challenges due to annotator perspectives influenced by their socio-economic backgrounds. For example, toxicity detection labels can vary significantly based on annotators’ racial identities (Sap et al. 2019). Researchers have addressed this inherent subjectivity in annotation processes by choosing between descriptive approaches that capture diverse perspectives or prescriptive approaches that enforce consistent interpretation (Rottger et al. 2022). Although neither approach is inherently superior, prescriptive approaches are particularly valuable in management research, where the goal is often to extract information aligned with precise, unified definitions of concepts.

The importance of prescriptive guidelines becomes magnified when transitioning from human to LLM annotators due to fundamental differences in information processing. Human annotators can seek clarification during ambiguous cases and rely on contextual understanding beyond the written guidelines (Salehi et al. 2017). In contrast, LLMs operate exclusively on textual input without the ability to request clarification or access implicit domain knowledge (Pryzant et al. 2023). This creates a critical asymmetry: whereas human annotation benefits from concise guidelines to maintain attention and reduce cognitive load (Snow et al. 2008), LLMs perform optimally with detailed, exhaustive instructions that anticipate edge cases and provide explicit decision rules. Consequently, the prescriptive approach becomes not merely preferable but essential for LLM annotation, as ambiguities in guidelines directly translate to increased measurement error without the possibility of real-time resolution.

Researchers have established that the prescriptive approach requires an iterative development process. For instance, Lee et al. (2023) emphasize continuous refinement through documented discussions among annotators. This collaborative approach achieves substantial agreement on the intended interpretation, achieved after resolving some edge cases of interpretation. For LLM applications, this iterative refinement process becomes even more critical because models cannot adapt their interpretation mid-task, making comprehensive guideline development the primary mechanism for reducing guideline-induced measurement error.

While these principles are established for human annotation processes, their application to LLM-based annotation introduces new challenges such as model selection or a requirement of carefully crafted “meta” system prompts that help models understand tasks and return results in structured, usable formats. Literature remains sparse on the adoption of well-established principles of reducing measurement error due to annotation guidelines when using LLMs for annotation.

### 2.2 LLMs for Text Annotation

Given that LLMs are trained on vast volumes of human-generated text, researchers have explored their capacity to replicate or augment human judgment across various domains. Early studies document that LLMs, such as GPT-3.5, could replace human coders for psychological construct detection (Rathje et al. 2024), policy interpretation (Leek et al. 2024), or act as experimental subjects or agents (Doshi et al. 2024, Xie et al. 2024, Yeykelis et al. 2025).

For text annotation specifically, where the objective is not to mimic human cognition but to produce consistent labels for clearly specified tasks, LLMs have shown strong promise (Tan et al. 2024). Gilardi et al. (2023) found zero-shot ChatGPT labeling achieved higher accuracy in political science classification tasks than crowdsourced workers. Mousavi et al. (2024) demonstrated that GPT-4 equals or surpasses traditional lexicon-based, supervised learning, and embedding approaches in psychometric text analysis. These findings suggest LLMs can serve as cost-effective alternatives to human annotation under certain conditions.

Several frameworks have emerged to guide LLM annotation pipeline. Pangakis et al. (2023) propose validation protocols against human labels and model selection procedures. Törnberg (2024) offer general implementation guidelines focusing on prompt engineering and evaluation metrics. de Kok (2025) present structured approaches to ChatGPT deployment for annotation tasks. However, a crucial gap in the literature is the lack of systematic attention to multiple aspects of LLM annotation (prescriptive annotation guidelines, baseline creation, meta prompt optimization, and rigorous model selection), each of which can introduce measurement error. As highlighted in Table 1, prior work seldom considers all four aspects together or targets error reduction across them. \OneAndAHalfSpacedXI

### 2.3 Robust Reproducibility and Model Confidence

Reproducibility requires that independent researchers can obtain consistent results using the same methodology (Fišar et al. 2024). The rapid evolution of LLMs introduces two previously unaddressed methodological challenges: determining when model confidence warrants generating multiple labels per instance, and ensuring robust reproducibility as proprietary models face retirement cycles. We define robust reproducibility as the ability to reproduce annotations under differing models. Proprietary models frequently become unavailable or deprecated, threatening the long-term reproducibility of research findings (Palmer et al. 2023). Unlike traditional statistical methods that remain stable across decades, LLM behaviors have been shown to vary drastically between adjacent versions (Chen et al. 2023). Since existing reproducibility frameworks in computational social science do not address these LLM-specific challenges, LLM-based analyses face fundamental reproducibility constraints when the underlying models become inaccessible. Furthermore, open-parameter models (such as GPT-OSS-120B) and proprietary models exhibit different levels of transparency and long-term availability. Understanding these differences becomes essential for developing annotation protocols that balance immediate quality with long-term reproducibility.

Model confidence presents additional methodological challenges that intersect with both measurement error and cost considerations. While Ipeirotis et al. (2014) demonstrate that generating multiple labels per instance can improve annotation quality when human annotator confidence is low, LLM annotation requires new approaches for measuring model confidence and determining optimal thresholds. Unlike human annotators who can express uncertainty explicitly, LLMs require post-hoc confidence estimation methods such as First-Second Distance metrics to identify when additional model votes may be warranted.

Current annotation frameworks lack systematic approaches to confidence-based annotation strategies and statistical equivalence testing between models. The absence of cost-effective methods for determining confidence thresholds and regression-based approaches for assessing model substitutability creates methodological gaps that limit both the efficiency and long-term scientific reliability of LLM-based annotation research.

### 3.2 Measurement Error Reduction Mechanisms

Our design approach, which we call SILICON (Systematic Inference with LLMs for Information Classification and Notation) systematically isolates and quantifies the four sources of measurement error identified in Section 3.1. The design follows three core principles.

-
1.
We isolate individual error sources through controlled comparisons that hold other factors constant, enabling attribution of performance differences to specific methodological choices.

-
2.
We maintain verbatim guideline integrity across all treatments to ensure that observed differences reflect genuine methodological improvements rather than instruction variations.

-
3.
We establish statistical equivalence criteria for robust reproducibility, addressing the model retirement problem that threatens long-term research validity.


Appendix Figure C1 illustrates our four-stage protocol, where each stage targets a specific measurement error source. The architecture enables both sequential implementation for optimal error reduction and modular application based on existing research infrastructure. Details of each component’s theoretical motivation, protocol design, and measurement strategy are below.

#### 3.2.1 Preliminary: measuring agreement.

Evaluating LLMs against human baselines requires a performance metric that captures annotation agreement and supports IAA analysis.
Several established metrics exist for evaluating IAA, such as Cohen’s Kappa (Cohen 1968), Fleiss’ Kappa (Fleiss 1971), and Krippendorff’s Alpha (Hayes and Krippendorff 2007). The choice of metric often depends on the characteristics of the annotation task and no single metric fits all contexts.
We consistently use Cohen’s Kappa (), which measures the level of agreement between two annotators while adjusting for chance agreement (Cohen 1968). Formally, it is given by:
,
where represents the relative observed agreement among raters, and denotes the hypothetical probability of agreement by chance.
We choose this metric for three main reasons. First, Cohen’s Kappa is designed for pairwise agreement analysis, which aligns with our objective of comparing a single LLM against the human baseline.
Second, it can be extended to scenarios involving multiple annotators through calculation and averaging of pairwise Kappa scores. This is useful during the phases of annotation guideline development and human baseline establishment, where evaluation typically involves more than two human annotators.
Third, it can be adapted to multi-label classification tasks, where items may belong to multiple categories simultaneously.555By incorporating context-dependent weighting matrices during the calculation, the weighted Cohen’s Kappa metric enables assessment of agreement across multi-label classification tasks. We provide detailed specifications of this adaptation in Appendix 7.1.

Ideally, the agreement metric should be as high as possible, but practical constraints often lead researchers to predetermine a threshold as an acceptable target. Here, we do not argue for the universal applicability of any specific threshold, as such thresholds reflect a trade-off between rigor and feasibility and are domain-specific (Paun et al. 2022). A commonly referenced threshold suggests that values above 0.4 indicate “moderate agreement” (Landis and Koch 1977). We set a target Cohen’s Kappa threshold of 0.5, which incorporates a conservative buffer of 0.1 to account for potential variability and uncertainty in determining moderate agreement. As discussed in Section 3.1, this threshold also serves as an empirical cutoff where co-labeling covariance effects are low.

#### 3.2.2 Guideline-induced error reduction.

Ambiguous annotation criteria create systematic measurement error as annotators apply inconsistent interpretations to edge cases. For LLM annotation, this problem becomes more acute because models cannot seek clarification during annotation, making explicit guidelines the sole mechanism for consistent interpretation (Törnberg 2024). Extant literature acknowledges the importance of detailed guidelines for human annotation tasks (Sheng et al. 2008, Lee et al. 2023) and shows that iterative refinement improves consistency (Hovy and Lavid 2010). Yet many LLM annotation studies adopt existing guidelines directly or draft new ones in a one-shot fashion (Gilardi et al. 2023, Rathje et al. 2024), risking guideline-induced error.

Protocol design. We compare iteratively refined guidelines against one-shot guidelines adapted from existing research. The iterative refinement follows a structured protocol based on established annotation science (Lee et al. 2023), where multiple annotators independently apply preliminary definitions, discuss disagreements through documented conversations (e.g., recorded Zoom call), and refine guidelines until achieving predetermined IAA thresholds. Appendix Figure C2 presents our guideline development protocol. In brief, annotators independently annotate initial samples, measure IAA against predefined thresholds, conduct documented discussions focusing on disagreements, and iterate until achieving consistent agreement on new samples. This process continues until annotators achieve the agreement threshold on first pass with a fresh subsample of data.

Measurement strategy. We operationalize guideline-induced error reduction through Cohen’s comparisons between iteratively refined and one-shot guidelines, holding constant the evaluation baseline,666We do not differentiate between expert- and crowd-based implementations for this step; the development of expert baselines is detailed in Section 3.2.3. meta-prompt structure, and model selection.

#### 3.2.3 Baseline-induced error reduction.

Human annotation baselines serve as the reference standard against which LLM annotations are evaluated, making baseline quality crucial for valid performance assessment. The choice between expert and crowdsourced annotators involves fundamental trade-offs. Domain experts bring specialized knowledge and can apply nuanced judgment (Snow et al. 2008), but are costly to recruit and may introduce systematic biases when their shared training leads to correlated errors (Aroyo and Welty 2015). Crowdsourced workers offer scalability and diverse perspectives (Ipeirotis et al. 2014), but typically receive minimal training and lack deep understanding of annotation guidelines (Snow et al. 2008, Zhang et al. 2023), creating measurement error in the evaluation process itself.

Protocol design. A key challenge in getting expert-generated baselines is the infeasibility of recruiting domain experts in many scenarios, due to time and cost considerations. The SILICON framework addresses this challenge by creating task-specific “annotation experts” through its iterative and collaborative prescriptive guideline development process. The task-specific “annotation experts” are individuals who participated in the iterative guideline development process and demonstrated consistent understanding of task definitions through high IAA. Having internalized consistent interpretations through the collaborative development process, they reduce evaluation-driven measurement error by minimizing disagreements about ambiguous cases that could confound LLM performance assessment. The protocol compares expert-generated baselines against crowdsourced baselines using identical annotation guidelines and evaluation protocols.

Measurement strategy. We assess baseline quality through internal consistency (mean among annotators). Sample sizes ranging from 120 to 200 items provide adequate statistical power while maintaining practical feasibility (Lee et al. 2023).

#### 3.2.4 Prompt-induced error reduction.

Meta-prompt structure affects LLM annotation performance even when guidelines remain verbatim constant, creating prompt-induced measurement error. To ensure fair comparisons between LLMs and human annotators, annotation guidelines should be incorporated verbatim into LLM prompts, with optimization focused solely on meta-prompt elements. Prior work suggests structure and reasoning strategies can influence outputs (Törnberg 2024, Wei et al. 2022).

Protocol design. We implement controlled meta-prompt optimization while preserving guideline integrity. Optimization focuses on three elements: (1) strategic positioning of annotation guidelines within prompt structure (system prompt versus user/human prompt), (2) adoption of task-relevant personas to align model perspective with domain expectations (Hu and Collier 2024), and (3) incorporation of reasoning strategies such as chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al. 2022).

The experimental protocol maintains strict separation between guideline content and meta-prompt elements. Guidelines are incorporated verbatim into all prompt variations, ensuring that performance differences reflect meta-prompt optimization rather than instruction changes. This design principle enables fair comparison between human and LLM annotation performance.

Measurement strategy. We quantify prompt-induced error reduction by comparing optimized meta-prompts against baseline prompt structure, holding guidelines, human baselines, and model selection constant. Observed paired contrasts identify corresponding improvements with respect to truth by Equation (4).

#### 3.2.5 Model-induced error assessment.

Different LLMs exhibit varying annotation performance due to architectural differences, training data variations, and alignment strategies (Mousavi et al. 2024). Model-induced error arises from this heterogeneity. Our approach addresses a critical question: do annotation results remain stable across different models? If outcomes are consistent across multiple high-performing models, then downstream analyses do not depend on idiosyncrasies of single model implementations. This establishes flexibility in model selection based on accessibility, cost, or computational requirements while maintaining annotation quality.

Protocol design. We evaluate multiple state-of-the-art LLMs using identical guidelines, baselines, and meta-prompts to isolate model-specific performance differences. The evaluation includes both proprietary models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro) and open-parameter ones (GPT-OSS-120B, LLaMA 3.3 70B, DeepSeek R1) to address reproducibility concerns (see Section 3.3).

Measurement strategy using statistical equivalence testing. We employ a regression-based framework to test for statistical equivalence777Statistical equivalence is defined as producing annotation outcomes that do not differ significantly in agreement metrics relative to human baselines. in model outputs. Since evaluation samples are randomly drawn from the population of interest, models producing statistically indistinguishable results on representative samples maintain similar performance when scaled to larger datasets.

Each model represents a distinct treatment, with item-treatment level annotations as the unit of analysis. The dependent variable indicates agreement between model annotation and human ground truth (binary). We perform logistic regression with treatment indicators, clustering standard errors at the item level to account for repeated-measures structure. The regression equation is presented in Section 5.5, with more details provided in Appendix 7.2. When observed contrasts are positive and the change in co-labeling covariance is sufficiently small, Equation (4) implies strictly reduced measurement error. Beyond identifying which models perform best, Section 3.3.2 addresses when model confidence warrants generating multiple labels per instance rather than relying on a single model’s output.

### 3.3 Robust Reproducibility Protocol

#### 3.3.1 Model confidence assessment.

Model confidence serves as a proxy for annotation reliability, enabling cost-sensitive strategies where uncertain predictions receive additional scrutiny. Unlike human annotators who can express uncertainty explicitly, LLMs require post-hoc confidence estimation methods. High-confidence predictions typically correlate with higher accuracy, making confidence assessment crucial for identifying when additional model votes or human review may be warranted (Lyu et al. 2025)

We evaluate intrinsic model reliability using the First-Second Distance (FSD) method (Lyu et al. 2025). FSD measures the discrepancy between the most common and second most common outputs across multiple generations from the same model. For each item, we generate five independent responses using temperature = 1, then calculate the difference between the most frequent response and the second most frequent response.888Here we obtain FSD scores by sampling; Appendix 7.3 details how to compute FSD from token-level log probabilities. A larger FSD indicates higher confidence, suggesting the model’s responses concentrate on a single answer across multiple runs.

#### 3.3.2 Multi-model annotation strategy.

Following Ipeirotis et al. (2014), adding multiple annotators is most valuable when existing labels show uncertainty. Running multiple models on every item yields high-quality labels but can be prohibitively expensive. Conversely, relying on a single model is cost-effective but error-prone. The optimal strategy balances cost against quality by strategically deploying multiple models based on confidence indicators.

Protocol design. The threshold selection strategy depends on three factors: budget constraints, quality requirements, and task-specific error costs. Researchers should first establish whether their focal model is a cost-effective option (typically open-parameter) or a high-performing proprietary model, as this determines the appropriate threshold range.

We recommend empirical calibration using the expert-annotated baseline as the validation sample: compute FSD distributions for your focal model, test 2-3 threshold values, and select the threshold that achieves acceptable quality improvements within budget constraints. The optimal threshold balances marginal quality gains against incremental annotation costs.

Measurement strategy. We evaluate threshold performance by varying across [0,1] interval and measuring both quality improvements and cost implications. Quality is assessed through Cohen’s Kappa against human ground truth, comparing single-model performance against multi-model performance triggered at different thresholds. Cost is operationalized as the fraction of items requiring additional model labels . The analysis identifies threshold ranges where marginal quality gains justify incremental costs.

#### 3.3.3 Open-parameter model substitution for robust reproducibility.

Proprietary model retirement threatens research reproducibility, as findings based on deprecated models cannot be replicated by future researchers. Open-parameter models provide permanent accessibility but may exhibit different performance characteristics than proprietary alternatives. Establishing statistical equivalence between open-parameter and proprietary models enables reproducible annotation pipelines that maintain quality while ensuring long-term availability.

Protocol design. We test whether high-performing open-parameter models can substitute proprietary models without significant quality loss. Using our regression-based equivalence testing framework, we compare open-parameter models (GPT-OSS-120B, LLaMA 3.3 70B, DeepSeek R1) against proprietary baselines (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) across all validation tasks.

Measurement strategy. Statistical equivalence is established when the confidence intervals for the performance difference encompass zero, thus indicating that there is no significant quality gap. Models achieving equivalence provide reproducible alternatives to proprietary options, enabling long-term research sustainability despite model retirement cycles.

### 3.4 Toolkit and Implementation

We have created an open-source toolkit that operationalizes SILICON, which we will release upon publication to respect the double-blind process. The toolkit includes utilities for agreement calculation for guideline refinement and baseline establishment; automated pipelines to compare different meta-prompt settings and multiple models; modules for model-confidence estimation and multi-LLM annotation; and statistical tests for robust reproducibility and equivalence.

## 4 Empirical Validation Design

We validate the SILICON methodology across seven annotation cases that are representative scenarios in management research. Our evaluation design employs two categories of validation approaches based on the level of methodological control achievable for each error source.

### 4.1 Full Methodological Control (Primary Cases).

The first category comprised four scenarios: business proposal evaluation, review attribute detection, dialog intent classification and breakdown analysis, and connectedness presence detection and classification. For these scenarios, we implemented the complete SILICON workflow, developing the annotation guidelines iteratively and establishing annotation-expert-validated human baselines with three research assistants per task.
The second category comprised three supplementary scenarios: language toxicity detection, criticism stance detection, and sentiment analysis. For this category, we adopted annotation guidelines and human baselines directly from published papers. Whereas this approach offers valuable comparative insights, it presents limitations-particularly our inability to verify the original IAA or whether the baselines were derived from expert or crowdsourced annotations.
Consequently, we tread these scenarios as supplementary evidence, drawing our primary conclusions from the first four scenarios.
Appendix 8 presents a summary of original research questions, annotation approaches, SILICON process implementation, and key findings for each case, and Online Appendix presents corresponding prompts.999Link to Online Appendix: https://drive.google.com/file/d/14sFKxeSANFX3Xl-umVxGNR_6qKZ5_M5Y/view?usp=sharing (This file is anonymous and non-tracking ).

#### 4.1.1 Business proposal evaluation.

Business documentation analysis, particularly of proposals, crowdfunding initiatives, and corporate statements, plays a critical role in conveying business-related information and is essential for analyzing organizational decision making and strategic behavior (Cao et al. 2019). In this case study, we focus on the classification of decentralized autonomous organization (DAO) business proposals, building on the work of Obermeier and Mayya (2024). This classification task involves categorizing user “proposals” based on their primary function or intention. Each proposal was categorized into one of six categories: Organizational, Business Model, Marketing, Functionality, Security, or Other. The categorization process aims to reveal patterns in how DAOs delegate and structure decision rights across their platforms.

#### 4.1.2 Review attribute detection.

Online reviews contain critical information that help the understanding of consumer purchase decisions. We obtained the annotated dataset from Liu et al. (2019), where authors used a large scale deep learning approach to identify the presence of six attribute in the product reviews, including price, performance feature, relatability/durability, conformance, aesthetics, and perceived quality. This is a multi-label classification task which provides insights into how different product attributes influence consumer decision-making.

#### 4.1.3 Dialog intent classification and breakdown analysis.

Dialog analysis has been critical in various domains, particularly in understanding and improving human-computer interaction.
We focus on two critical aspects of dialog analysis: dialog intent classification (Stolcke et al. 2000) and breakdown analysis (Higashinaka et al. 2016), using a sample of customer service dialog data obtained from a Hugging Face dataset.101010https://huggingface.co/datasets/bitext/Bitext-customer-support-llm-chatbot-training-dataset
The first task, dialog intent classification, requires human annotators to classify the intention of each utterance into one or multiple categories (i.e., multi-label classification): factual questions, yes/no questions, task commands, invalid commands, appreciations, complaints, comments, statement non-opinions, positive answers, and negative answers.
The second task, the dialog breakdown analysis, focuses on identifying whether an utterance in the conversation leads to a breakdown, classifying each utterance as: (1) not a breakdown, (2) a possible breakdown, or (3) confirmed breakdown.

#### 4.1.4 Affective content evaluation (connectedness presence and classification).

Affective content in marketing—such as in advertisements, product packaging, and product descriptions—plays a significant role in shaping consumer decision-making (Paharia et al. 2011). Evaluating affective content is therefore critical for understanding consumer behavior. In this study, we focus on one specific dimension of affective content: the sense of connectedness. We use a dataset from Cheng et al. (2024), which investigates the presence and nature of connectedness in online product descriptions. The first task, connectedness presence detection, is a binary classification task where human annotators assess whether a product description conveys a sense of connectedness or not. The second task, connectedness classification, is conducted only when connectedness is present. This is a multi-label classification task where each product description may be assigned one or more of the following categories: Emotional Appeal, Storytelling, Relatable Scenarios, Empathy, and Cultural or Community Connection.

### 4.2 Limited Methodological Control (Complementary Cases).

#### 4.2.1 Language toxicity detection.

Detecting toxic content in textual data plays a critical role in management research, offering insights into a range of organizational and social dynamics. Toxic interactions, such as hate speech or fear-based messaging, can significantly impact online communities (Matook et al. 2022, Sibai et al. 2024), and organizational behavior (Rosette et al. 2013). For this task, we utilize the pre-existing annotation guidelines, human baseline, and raw data publicly available from Saha et al. (2023). The annotated items are social media posts from Gab. The task is to mark each post as a) fear speech, b) hate speech, c) normal, or d) both fear speech and hate speech (if the post contains elements of both).

#### 4.2.2 Criticism stance detection.

We selected this case because the core task—criticism stance detection—can be generalized to address a broad range of organizational and social challenges. Specifically, we use data from Peng et al. (2022), which focuses on detecting the criticism stance of tweets about certain academic papers, framing it as a binary classification task.

#### 4.2.3 Sentiment analysis.

Sentiment analysis plays a pivotal role in management research, with applications across various contexts such as social media platforms (Zhang et al. 2016, Oh et al. 2023, Tang et al. 2024), e-commerce platforms (Homburg et al. 2015), and firm-public communications (Choudhury et al. 2019). In this study, we assess whether text annotations generated by LLMs can produce similarly well-aligned results. For this task, we utilize annotation guidelines, human baselines, and raw data from Sen et al. (2020).

### 4.3 Prompt and Model Specifics

The prompt strategies included a base prompt, a prompt with persona settings, and a prompt with chain-of-thought, all unified in their placement within the system role rather than the user role (for reasons that will appear in Section 5.3). These prompts were initially tested using GPT-4o to establish a benchmark.
Based on the results from GPT-4o, we identified the optimal prompt by balancing performance and cost considerations.
This optimal prompt was then applied across several models: GPT-4o, o3-mini, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro, LLaMA 3.3 70B, DeepSeek-R1, and GPT-OSS-120B.111111We used the following versions of models: GPT-4o-2024-08-06, o3-mini-2025-01-31, Claude-3-5-Sonnet-20240620, Gemini-1.5-pro, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1, and GPT-OSS-120B.

## 5 Empirical Validation Results

We present results in the same sequence as described in Section 3.1.3: guideline contrast, reference baseline contrast, meta prompt contrast, and model contrast. We then evaluate robust reproducibility protocols and multi-LLM annotation strategies. Our empirical validation demonstrates systematic measurement error reduction across all four sources, with each intervention targeting distinct aspects of the annotation process.

### 5.1 Reducing Guideline-induced Error

Ambiguous or incomplete annotation guidelines can create systematic measurement error when annotators apply inconsistent interpretations. We examine whether iterative guideline refinement reduces this source of error by comparing LLM annotation performance using one-shot (pre-existing) guidelines versus iteratively refined ones developed through our structured protocol. Figure 2 presents Cohen’s Kappa values between LLM annotations and expert-generated ground truth across six tasks. LLM performance was consistently lower when using one-shot guidelines compared to iteratively refined guidelines. The improvement ranged from 0.1–0.5 Kappa points, with the largest gains observed in dialog intent classification and breakdown analysis tasks, where initial agreement levels below 0.1 (indicating no meaningful agreement) improved to fair agreement level after guideline refinement.

These findings provide strong support for the argument that holding human baseline procedures (), meta-prompts (), and models () constant while anchoring evaluation at refined guidelines (), the transition from to increases observed agreement (). Appendix Figure C4 illustrates the gains from iterative refinement process, showing that IAA among annotation experts rises consistently over multiple revision rounds. Achieving high IAA typically requires several iterations for complex tasks, supporting our framework that prescriptive guidelines must be systematically developed rather than created in isolation.

### 5.2 Reducing Baseline-induced Error

Unreliable human reference standards introduce systematic baseline-induced error when the evaluation standard itself diverges from ground truth. We test whether expert-generated baselines reduce this source of error by comparing the internal consistency of annotation experts versus crowdsourced workers using identical annotation guidelines.

For each of the four primary cases (comprising six sub-tasks), we constructed two distinct annotation baselines using our finalized annotation guidelines. The expert baseline was obtained from three undergraduate research assistants who participated in the iterative guideline development process, while the crowdsourced baseline was obtained from three different research assistants who received the guidelines without participating in their development. Both groups annotated 200 to 300 randomly chosen documents using identical protocols. Figure 3 presents the IAA comparisons between the two baseline procedures. The annotation experts consistently achieved higher consensus compared to crowdsourced annotators across all six tasks. For instance, in the dialog intent classification task, the mean Cohen’s among expert annotators was 0.61 (indicating substantial agreement), whereas crowdsourced annotators achieved only 0.23, reflecting weaker alignment and less consistent understanding of the annotation criteria.

title: Bias and Unfairness in Information Retrieval Systems: New Challenges in the LLM Era
description: Comprehensive survey on bias and unfairness issues in IR systems integrated with LLMs, covering emerging challenges from distribution mismatch.

# Bias and Unfairness in Information Retrieval Systems:

New Challenges in the LLM Era

###### Abstract.

With the rapid advancements of large language models (LLMs), information retrieval (IR) systems, such as search engines and recommender systems, have undergone a significant paradigm shift. This evolution, while heralding new opportunities, introduces emerging challenges, particularly in terms of biases and unfairness, which may threaten the information ecosystem. In this paper, we present a comprehensive survey of existing works on emerging and pressing bias and unfairness issues in IR systems when the integration of LLMs. We first unify bias and unfairness issues as distribution mismatch problems, providing a groundwork for categorizing various mitigation strategies through distribution alignment. Subsequently, we systematically delve into the specific bias and unfairness issues arising from three critical stages of LLMs integration into IR systems: data collection, model development, and result evaluation. In doing so, we meticulously review and analyze recent literature, focusing on the definitions, characteristics, and corresponding mitigation strategies associated with these issues. Finally, we identify and highlight some open problems and challenges for future work, aiming to inspire researchers and stakeholders in the IR field and beyond to better understand and mitigate bias and unfairness issues of IR in this LLM era. We also consistently maintain a GitHub repository for the relevant papers and resources in this rising direction at https://github.com/KID-22/LLM-IR-Bias-Fairness-Survey.

## 1. Introduction

Information Retrieval (IR) systems strive to navigate the era of information overload, facilitating users in acquiring information more efficiently and effectively (Xu et al., 2018; Singhal et al., 2001; Manning, 2009). The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) has fundamentally redefined IR systems, including the introduction of LLM-generated data as new IR data sources, the shift from passive retrieval to proactive generation as core paradigms, and adopting LLMs as results evaluators for IR systems (Zhu et al., 2023; Ai et al., 2023). These advancements, however, bring forth new challenges in bias and unfairness, affecting the reliability of IR systems and potentially contributing to societal issues like echo chambers (Del Vicario et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2024) and cognitive interference (Sarason et al., 2014; Mihaylov et al., 2018). For instance, researchers found that LLMs often retrieve information that deviates from facts and is biased towards LLM-generated content (Dai et al., 2024b; Xu et al., 2023b; Li et al., 2023b; Chern et al., 2023). Moreover, LLMs frequently manifest stereotypes and discriminatory content to users and amplify disparities between items of different socio-economic statuses (Zhang et al., 2023a; Xu et al., 2023d; Jiang et al., 2024a).

Recently, much effort has been made around bias and unfairness in the context of LLMs and IR systems. However, the literature is currently fragmented and often lacks a unified definition of these concepts. This ambiguity hampers the development of systematic strategies to address these issues effectively. To this end, our survey aims to provide a comprehensive and unified perspective that effectively summarizes the emerging challenges and opportunities related to bias and unfairness in the intersection between LLMs and IR systems. Generally, both bias and unfairness issues can be regarded as a distribution mismatch problem. Specifically, bias underscores the fact that the predicted information lacks objectivity and truthfulness, highlighting the mismatch with the objective target distribution. Unfairness reveals that the predicted information fails to align with the social values between humans and machines, leading to a mismatch with the subjective target distribution of human values. This perspective not only unifies the nature of these issues but also streamlines the exploration of mitigation strategies.

Our survey begins with a brief overview of how LLMs are integrated into IR systems, setting the stage for understanding the emergence of new bias and unfairness challenges across three pivotal stages of the IR lifecycle: data collection, model development, and result evaluation. Then we propose a unified perspective on bias and unfairness, categorizing them as distribution mismatch problems. Based on this unified view, we categorize mitigation strategies into two principal groups: data sampling, including data augmentation and data filtering, and distribution reconstruction, encompassing rebalancing, regularization, and prompting. Following this taxonomy, we delve into a detailed analysis of several types of bias and unfairness phenomena that arise with the integration of LLMs into IR systems, spanning the aforementioned stages. Our systematic review encompasses a comprehensive examination of these issues and their respective mitigation strategies in recent studies, providing a holistic view of the current landscape and guiding future efforts in eliminating bias and ensuring fairness for more trustworthy IR systems.

Difference with Existing Surveys. Several recent surveys have reviewed and discussed the issues of bias and fairness within IR (Chen et al., 2023a; Wang et al., 2023d; Li et al., 2023a; Zehlike et al., 2021; Pitoura et al., 2022), primarily focusing on works published before the advent of LLMs. With LLMs becoming increasingly prevalent, a new subset of surveys (Gallegos et al., 2023; Xue et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023c; Li et al., 2023c) has paid attention to the bias and fairness challenges presented by LLMs themselves. Additionally, some other recent surveys (Ai et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023c; Lin et al., 2023) have examined how integrating LLMs can enhance and transform traditional IR systems, highlighting some opportunities arising from this integration. Compared to these surveys, our work stands apart by offering a comprehensive survey of the emerging and pressing issues of bias and fairness at the intersection of IR and LLMs, employing a novel unified perspective to review the cause and mitigation strategies.

Summary of Contributions. (1) We provide a novel unified perspective for understanding bias and unfairness as distribution mismatch problems, alongside a detailed review of several types of bias and unfairness arising from integrating LLMs into IR systems. (2) We systematically organize mitigation strategies into two key categories: data sampling and distribution reconstruction, offering a comprehensive roadmap for effectively combating bias and unfairness with state-of-the-art approaches. (3) We identify the current challenges and future directions, providing insights to facilitate the development of this potential and demanding research area.

## 2. A Unified View of Bias and Unfairness

In this section, we provide a unified view of bias and unfairness from the perspective of distribution alignment and outline the mitigation strategies based on this view.

### 2.1. Background

As shown in Figure 1, the advent of LLMs has reshaped the whole pipeline of IR systems, typically in the following three stages: data collection, model development, and result evaluation.

LLMs-generated content as new data sources for IR. The emergence of LLMs has significantly accelerated the growth of Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC), marking a new era in content creation. Unlike traditional Professional and User Generated Content (PGC and UGC) sources, AIGC can be produced automatically at scale, potentially dominating the content landscape. (Cao et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023a; Hanley and Durumeric, 2023). However, AIGC also reshapes the distribution of the IR data, resulting in new concerns about bias and fairness.

Incorporating LLMs to enhance or as IR models. The impressive emergent capabilities of LLMs in understanding, reasoning, and generalization have motivated significant efforts to integrate them into the development of next-generation IR systems (Zhu et al., 2023). On one hand, LLMs have been deployed to refine key components of traditional IR systems (Sun et al., 2023; Shi and Min, 2023; Wang et al., 2023g), enhancing their effectiveness and efficiency. On the one hand, beyond enhancing existing frameworks, LLMs also introduce a novel paradigm by acting as generative search and recommendation agents (Nakano et al., 2021; Gur et al., 2023; Dai et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023e), directly generating responses to fulfill user queries.

Adopting LLMs as results evaluators in IR systems. Human evaluation plays a pivotal role in IR systems, particularly in conversational search and recommendation, such as directly assessing the quality of responses from generative LLM-based IR models (Dai et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023h; Zheng et al., 2023b). However, human evaluation comes with significant challenges, including high costs and a lack of reproducibility. LLMs, with their advanced language modeling and understanding capabilities, offer new possibilities for conducting evaluations of these complex tasks without human evaluation (Chiang and Lee, 2023; Svikhnushina and Pu, 2023; Li et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2024). This shift not only streamlines the evaluation process but also mitigates the substantial costs associated with human evaluations, further facilitating the development of IR systems.

### 2.2. Distribution Alignment Perspective

While the reshaping of the above IR stages by LLMs has introduced numerous new opportunities, it has also given rise to many new and pressing issues related to bias and unfairness. In this section, we formulate the problems of bias and fairness from a distribution alignment perspective, offering a unified framework for understanding these challenges and inspiring mitigation strategies.

Formally, when a user interacts with a typical IR system, he/she may optionally provide his/her personalized information requirement along with their personalized attributes (typically indicated as user profile ) to the system. Subsequently, the goal of the IR system is to retrieve the target information (*e.g., *documents, items, or advertisements, *et al. *) for this user, with the user’s information requirements and optional interaction history as the input . Let be the predicted result either from IR models or directly generated by LLMs, where is the model.

Let be the distribution of predicted results for all users, we can unify the bias and unfairness problem as a distribution mismatch problem with the ground truth distribution , where is the target result, which can be defined as follows:

| (1) |

Based on the Equation 1, the bias and unfairness problem can be explained as follows:

Bias stems from systemic deviations occurring at various stages of the IR process, from data collection to model design and evaluation. These systemic issues results in the predicted distribution, , diverging from the target distribution, , which ideally represents objective and factual realities.

Unfairness deeply rooted in cultural and societal notions of fairness, aims to align the predicted distribution with a subjective target distribution . It reflects human values and social contracts and evolves with the progress of time.

### 2.3. Taxonomies of Mitigation Strategies

Based on our unified view, we can further systematically categorize mitigation strategies from the view of distribution alignment. Specifically, the goal of mitigation strategies is to align the distribution of retrieved information with a target distribution defined by either objective criteria or subjective social values. As shown in Figure 2, we outline two primary categories and their sub-strategies:

(1) Data Sampling focuses on directly modifying the data:

Data Augmentation serves as distribution completion, enriching the dataset with additional, often synthetic, data to approximate the target distribution more closely. Techniques such as counterfactual imputation and the incorporation of external knowledge are employed to fill in the gaps in the existing dataset, thus aiming to recover the real distribution more accurately.

Data Filtering acts as distribution truncation, selecting data subsets that align with the target distribution, ensuring the model’s output is representative of desired target outcomes. Techniques like re-ranking and constrained beam search fall under this category, serving as post-processing methods to ensure the retained distribution segment matches the target distribution.

(2) Distribution Reconstruction aims at adjusting the predicted distribution:

Rebalancing transforms the predicted distribution through techniques like reweighting or resampling, to reflect the target distribution more accurately. Common strategies include adjusting the loss weights for various groups to achieve equilibrium, thereby realigning the predicted distribution with the target distribution.

Regularization narrows the predicted distribution by introducing constraints that encourage the model to learn the target distribution more faithfully. It encompasses both implicit approaches, such as adversarial learning, and explicit ones, like regularization techniques, to modify the distribution directly.

Prompting extracts the best aligned distribution by directly employing specific prompts. This approach guides LLMs to generate outputs more likely from the target distribution, facilitating an alignment with the desired target distribution.

Through the lens of distribution alignment, these strategies offer a structured and coherent approach to eliminate bias and ensure fairness of IR systems in IR systems. In the following sections, we will conduct a detailed review of various emerging issues related to bias and unfairness, their mitigation solutions, and their integration within the distribution alignment framework.

## 3. Cause and Mitigation of Bias

As summarized in Table 1, we present an in-depth review of different types of bias at the different stages of the intersection between LLMs and IR systems and discuss the corresponding mitigation strategies.
