The difference serves as a robust membership signal that does not solely depend on overfitting.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Key Findings Takeaway

The following key findings summarize the main trends observed in our experiments and provide guidance on the trade-offs between model utility and privacy protection:

-
(1)
Differential privacy reduces model utility, with lower privacy budgets causing greater degradation. Full fine-tuning and LoRA exhibit strong robustness, whereas prefix-tuning suffers significantly, particularly in larger models.

-
(2)
Without DP, full fine-tuning and LoRA are prone to extreme memorization, resulting in very high exposure and MIA risk, while prefix-tuning and P-tuning naturally offer better privacy protection.

-
(3)
With DP training, both exposure and MIA risk are significantly reduced across all methods, with full fine-tuning and LoRA benefiting most; however, further lowering the privacy budget has only marginal effects on MIA AUC.

-
(4)
In terms of privacy-utility trade-off, full fine-tuning achieves the best overall balance. Among the PEFT approaches, LoRA excels in preserving utility and P-tuning offers superior privacy protection, whereas prefix-tuning is not recommended due to its severe utility loss under DP.


### 4.2 Experimental Setup

#### 4.2.1 Environment.

The experiments were conducted on a Linux server running Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS. Our environment used Python 3.10 with PyTorch 1.13.0 and CUDA 11.6, alongside key libraries such as Transformers and fastDP. The server featured dual NVIDIA A6000 GPUs (totaling 96GB of VRAM), an AMD EPYC 7313P CPU, and 503GB of system memory, providing a robust platform for training and evaluating our models under differential privacy and various fine-tuning methods.

#### 4.2.2 Datasets.

In our study, we employed two datasets for fine-tuning the language model: Wikitext-2-v1 [23] and AG News [31]. Wikitext-2-v1 is a high-quality corpus derived from English Wikipedia articles. It contains 36718 samples for training and 3760 samples for validation. AG News is a widely recognized dataset used primarily for text classification tasks. It contains 120000 samples for training and is known for its concise yet diverse content.

For the data extraction attack, we utilize the entire Wikitext-2-v1. The canary sample is The secret code is hzdh0831. The method for constructing the training set is detailed in methodology. In the Membership Inference Attack, we extract 10,000 samples from the AG News’ train-set to form the training set, which represents the member set in the context of the attack. Additionally, we extract 1,000 samples from AG News’ test-set to serve as the evaluation set, which simultaneously functions as the non-member set.

#### 4.2.3 Models.

We employ two autoregressive language models: GPT-2 and GPT-2 XL [27]. GPT-2 is an autoregressive model based on the transformer architecture, pre-trained on a diverse corpus of web text. It is well-known for its ability to generate coherent and contextually relevant text, making it a popular choice for language modeling tasks. GPT-2 XL, the largest variant in the GPT-2 family, contains a significantly higher number of parameters, which allows it to capture more intricate language patterns and deliver enhanced performance on complex tasks. GPT-2 has 124M parameters while GPT-2 XL has 1.5B parameters.

For the fine-tuning methods, we adopt full fine-tuning as our baseline. Additionally, we explore three popular parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) approaches: prefix-tuning, LoRA, and P-tuning, which are detailed in Section 3. For PEFT of GPT-2, we use 8 as the rank of LoRA, 30 as the length of virtual tokens in Prefix-tuning and P-tuning, 128 as the size of hidden encoder in P-tuning. These methods are implemented using the peft [21] module available in the Transformers [29] library, enabling us to compare their performance in terms of utility and privacy risks. In two attack experiments, we fine-tuned for 10 epochs for the target model and used early-stopping to prevent overfitting.

#### 4.2.4 Differential Privacy Mechanism.

We employ DP-Adam to provide sample-level differential privacy protection for the fine-tuning dataset. Specifically, we utilize fastDP [6, 4, 3], a library that enables differentially private optimization of PyTorch models. FastDP implements gradient clipping based on Book-Keeping approach to achieve differential privacy. It can integrate seamlessly with our chosen PEFT methods and language models.

#### 4.2.5 Metrics.

For model utility analysis, we use perplexity as the evaluation metric in both experiments. In the prompt attack experiment, we measure the risk of privacy leakage using the exposure metric, which is detailed in Section 3. For the membership inference attack (MIA) experiment, we employ SPV-MIA as the attack method and assess its effectiveness using the AUC (Area Under the Curve) and ARC (Attack Success Rate) metrics.

### 4.3 Impact of Differential Privacy on Model Utility

We plotted the perplexity of fine-tuned models against different privacy budgets across two settings in Fig. 1. Without the application of differential privacy, all three PEFT methods exhibit perplexity levels comparable to full fine-tuning, with LoRA even matching the full fine-tuning performance. This indicates that, in the absence of DP, the selected PEFT approaches can maintain high utility, with LoRA showing the best performance.

However, once noise is introduced via differential privacy, the utility of the models degrades across all fine-tuning methods. As the privacy budget decreases (i.e., as more noise is injected), the perplexity of the models increases. We fine-tuned both GPT-2 and GPT-2 XL on Wikitext-v2. The results reveal that, with the exception of prefix-tuning, all fine-tuning methods yield lower perplexity on DP-trained GPT-2 XL compared to GPT-2, indicating enhanced utility for larger models. However, prefix-tuning exhibits the opposite behavior. GPT-2 XL fine-tuned with prefix-tuning shows higher perplexity, suggesting that differential privacy severely impacts its utility. The anomalous behavior of prefix-tuning on larger models warrants further investigation and validation. Notably, the extent of the perplexity’s increase varies among the methods; prefix-tuning shows the most pronounced deterioration in utility, while FFT and LoRA continue to maintain relatively good performance. A possible explanation for these observations is that methods like FFT and LoRA distribute the DP-induced noise across a larger set of parameters or incorporate it into low-rank updates, which mitigates its adverse effects. In contrast, prefix-tuning relies heavily on a small set of learned prompt representations to condition the model’s output. Consequently, the noise has a disproportionate impact on these few parameters, leading to a significant decline in their effectiveness and, therefore, a marked drop in utility.

###### Remark 1

Differential privacy reduces model utility, with lower privacy budgets causing greater degradation. LoRA and full fine-tuning are relatively robust, while prefix-tuning suffers severe utility loss. Notably, although larger models typically yield higher utility at the same privacy budget, prefix-tuning exhibits a counterintuitive drop.

### 4.4 Impact of Differential Privacy on Empirical Privacy Risk

To evaluate the impact of differential privacy on models’ empirical privacy risk. We performed two attacks on GPT-2 obtained by different fine-tuning methods which is detailed in Section 3.

#### 4.4.1 Data Extraction.

We plotted the exposure metric against the privacy budget for various fine-tuning methods in Fig. 2.

Without applying any DP mechanism, both FFT (full fine-tuning) and LoRA exhibit extremely high exposure, reaching the maximum possible level. This indicates that these models can directly output the secret code embedded in the canary, thus posing a significant privacy risk. An adversary can easily extract sensitive information by simply providing an appropriate prompt. In contrast, prefix-tuning and P-tuning inherently offer a degree of privacy protection, as their exposure is much lower than FFT and LoRA with no DP mechanism We hypothesize that it is related to the location of the fine-tuned parameters within the model. Methods like FFT and LoRA modify parameters that are distributed across key layers (such as the self-attention and feed-forward networks) which are directly involved in generating outputs and encoding detailed information from the training data. This broader and deeper integration allows these methods to capture and retain more specific patterns and even sensitive details. In contrast, techniques like prefix-tuning and P-tuning adjust only a small set of additional parameters—typically in the form of prompt embeddings or similar auxiliary tokens—that are less tightly coupled with the core model representations. This more limited and peripheral update results in a lower capacity for memorization.

After introducing DP noise, the results show distinct behaviors across the fine-tuning methods. For FFT and LoRA that tend to develop strong memorization of the training data, the application of DP leads to a significant reduction in exposure even at a high privacy budget (e.g., =50). This indicates that DP is highly effective in mitigating the memorization—and thus the privacy risk—of sensitive data in these models. Conversely, for prefix-tuning and P-tuning, although the introduction of DP noise does lower exposure, the reduction is less pronounced. We speculate that this may be because these two methods, particularly in smaller models like GPT-2, do not form strong memorization in the first place, leaving less room for DP to further reduce exposure. Furthermore, as the privacy budget decreases, there is a general trend of declining exposure, which suggests that a stricter privacy budget does indeed enhance privacy protection. However, compared to the initial drop in exposure observed when DP was first applied, the subsequent decreases are not as significant.

Another interesting finding is that, when mitigating prompt attacks, differential privacy proved more effective on GPT-2 XL than on GPT-2, as shown by a more pronounced decrease in exposure. One possible explanation is that larger models have more parameters, allowing them to better absorb and distribute the noise introduced by DP. This dilution of noise effects on individual parameters reduces the model’s tendency to memorize specific training data, thereby enhancing privacy protection under the same privacy budget.

###### Remark 2

Without differential privacy, full fine-tuning and LoRA result in very high exposure, which contradicts previous studies that reported LoRA as having the lowest exposure. In contrast, prefix-tuning and P-tuning naturally provide better privacy protection. When differential privacy is applied, exposure decreases significantly, and lower privacy budgets lead to even lower exposure. Moreover, more complete prompts tend to increase privacy risk. Larger models exhibit lower exposure than smaller ones under the same privacy budget.

#### 4.4.2 Membership Inference Attack.

In our MIA experiments, we observed some intriguing phenomena and we plot the results in Fig. 3. Without differential privacy (DP), both FFT and LoRA were extremely vulnerable to MIA, achieving AUC values exceeding 80% and FFT reaching as high as 97.8%, which clearly indicates a very high privacy risk. We attribute this vulnerability to the strong memorization capabilities inherent in FFT and LoRA, leading these methods to effectively capture and reproduce sensitive information from the training data. In contrast, prefix-tuning and P-tuning exhibited substantially lower AUC values (around 60%) in the absence of DP, consistent with our findings from the prompt attack experiments. To eliminate the influence of model architecture, we fine-tuned GPT-J [28] on the same dataset without differential privacy. The results show that GPT-J fine-tuned with P-tuning and prefix-tuning still maintains a low AUC of around 0.6 against SPV-MIA. These results suggest that prefix-tuning and P-tuning naturally offer a degree of privacy protection by limiting the memorization of individual training samples, which is consistent with our findings in the data extraction.

Upon introducing a differential privacy mechanism, all four fine-tuning methods experience a substantial reduction in AUC. In particular, FFT and LoRA see dramatic decreases, with all methods converging to approximately 58% AUC. We plotted the ROC curves of GPT-2 XL under SPV-MIA before and after DP training in Fig. 4. It can be seen that DP training significantly reduces the attack threat on LoRA and full fine-tuning.

However, further lowering the privacy budget beyond this point does not yield a more pronounced decline in AUC. One potential explanation for this plateau is that the initial application of differential privacy introduces enough noise to disrupt the memorization signals exploited by the attacks, effectively reducing vulnerability across the board. Once these signals are sufficiently obfuscated, additional noise, which is achieved by further lowering the privacy budget, offers diminishing returns in terms of additional privacy gains. In fact, even with a privacy budget of =1, differential privacy guarantees that the success rate of MIA remains below 73%, which is still higher than the AUC values observed in current MIAs. This may imply that current MIA methods are still insufficient in their ability to effectively attack models trained with differential privacy.

###### Remark 3

Without differential privacy, full fine-tuning and LoRA exhibit extremely high MIA risk, whereas prefix-tuning and P-tuning inherently offer some privacy protection, consistent with our previous findings. Once DP training is introduced, the MIA risk decreases for all fine-tuning methods, with reductions being particularly significant for full fine-tuning and LoRA. Notably, even at very high privacy budgets, DP still provides substantial protection against MIA, though further changes in the privacy budget have little impact on the AUC.

### 4.5 Trade-off between Utility and Privacy

Achieving an optimal trade-off between utility and privacy remains a critical objective. To evaluate how different fine-tuning methods balance utility and privacy protection under differential privacy (DP), we plotted the relationship between exposure and perplexity as well as AUC and perplexity for each fine-tuning method, as shown in Fig. 5. In these plots, every point on a curve corresponds to the model’s performance under a specific privacy budget. We interpret a better privacy-utility trade-off as a situation where a model maintains low perplexity while also keeping exposure and AUC low; therefore, curves that are generally closer to the lower-left corner indicate superior trade-offs. It is important to note that the rightmost point on each curve represents = (i.e., no DP), and when considering trade-offs under differential privacy, this point can be disregarded.

Based on the plots, under differential privacy the curves for full fine-tuning are consistently closer to the lower-left corner in both graphs. This indicates that full fine-tuning achieves the best privacy-utility trade-off under DP. We attribute this to the large number of trainable parameters in full fine-tuning, which enables the model to better absorb and mitigate the impact of DP-induced noise while still protecting privacy.

Among the PEFT methods, both LoRA and P-tuning demonstrate a favorable trade-off. Specifically, the curve for P-tuning is positioned further left, suggesting a stronger advantage in privacy protection, whereas the curve for LoRA is shifted slightly to the right, reflecting better utility preservation. In contrast, prefix-tuning under DP leads to excessively high perplexity, severely compromising model utility. Although it offers relatively strong privacy protection, the excessive loss in utility—likely due to the model’s diminished capacity to memorize—renders prefix-tuning unsuitable for DP training in its current form. This suggests a need for developing DP training methods tailored specifically for prefix-tuning.

In summary, full fine-tuning appears to be the best option under DP due to its high privacy-utility trade-off. However, given the substantial computational resources and time required for full fine-tuning, it is often impractical with large models. Among the PEFT approaches, LoRA is recommended when model utility is the primary concern, whereas P-tuning is preferable when stronger privacy protection is desired. We do not recommend using prefix-tuning under DP training because of its severe impact on utility. It is important to note that prefix-tuning and P-tuning naturally offer a certain degree of privacy protection even without DP. Therefore, if reducing privacy risk is the primary concern and DP training is not feasible, these methods are attractive alternatives.

###### Remark 4

Under differential privacy, full fine-tuning achieves the best privacy-utility trade-off, as it maintains low perplexity and low exposure/AUC. Among the PEFT methods, LoRA and P-tuning offer promising results. P-tuning excels in privacy protection, while LoRA better preserves utility. In contrast, prefix-tuning suffers from excessively high perplexity under DP, severely impairing utility, and is therefore not recommended. These findings suggest that while full fine-tuning is optimal, practical constraints make PEFT methods attractive; among them, LoRA is preferable when utility is paramount, and P-tuning when privacy is the main concern.

## 5 Future Work

While our study offers valuable insights into the impact of privacy budgets on model utility and protection across fine-tuning methods, it is limited in several ways. Our experiments focused solely on the GPT-2 family, which may not capture the full range of behaviors exhibited by other architectures or larger language models. Additionally, we limited our analysis to standard differentially private optimization algorithms, even though recent advances have introduced specialized DP methods for PEFT, such as RAFT [17], which might offer improved trade-offs between utility and privacy. Our exploration of PEFT parameter configurations was also restricted to a few settings, leaving open questions about how different configurations might affect model performance and privacy risk. Furthermore, our evaluation was based on a narrow set of datasets, which may not fully represent the diversity of real-world data distributions and their associated privacy challenges. Future work should address these limitations by incorporating a broader range of models, exploring diverse DP methods (especially those tailored for PEFT), systematically varying parameter settings, and utilizing more varied datasets to enhance the generalizability and robustness of the findings.

## 6 Conclusion

In this work, we investigated the impact of differential privacy on the utility and empirical privacy risk of large language models fine-tuned with various methods, including both full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods. Our experiments demonstrate that while differential privacy effectively reduces model exposure and membership inference risks, it also degrades utility, with the extent of degradation varying significantly across different fine-tuning methods. Moreover, our analysis of the privacy-utility trade-off reveals that, under DP, full fine-tuning achieves the best overall balance; however, practical considerations such as resource constraints make PEFT methods, particularly LoRA and P-tuning, attractive alternatives depending on whether the emphasis is on preserving utility or ensuring privacy. Overall, our findings provide valuable guidance for selecting fine-tuning strategies under DP constraints and set the stage for future research aimed at optimizing the trade-off between model performance and privacy protection in large-scale language models.

title: Secret Stealing Attacks on Local LLM Fine-Tuning through Supply-Chain Model Code Backdoors
description: Shows DP-SGD can create illusion of privacy protection. Model fine-tuned with DP retains pre-training knowledge but fails to learn from new data, masking privacy risks while appearing to work.
content:
# Secret Stealing Attacks on Local LLM Fine-Tuning through Supply-Chain Model Code Backdoors

###### Abstract

Local fine-tuning datasets routinely contain sensitive secrets such as API keys, personal identifiers, and financial records. Although “local offline fine-tuning” is often viewed as a privacy boundary, we reveal that compromised model code is sufficient to steal them. Current passive pretrained-weight poisoning attacks, while effective for natural language, fundamentally fail to capture such sparse high-entropy targets due to their reliance on probabilistic semantic prefixes. To bridge this gap, we identify and exploit a practical but overlooked supply-chain vector—model code camouflaged as standard architectural definitions—to realize a paradigm shift from passive weight poisoning to active execution hijacking. We introduce a deterministic full-chain memorization mechanism: it locks onto token-level secrets in dynamic computation flows via online tensor-rule matching, and leverages value–gradient decoupling to stealthily inject attack gradients, overcoming gradient drowning to force model memorization. Furthermore, we achieve, for the first time, attacker-verifiable secret stealing through black-box queries that precisely distinguishes true leakage from hallucination. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves over 98% Strict ASR without compromising the primary task, and can effectively bypass defense measures including DP-SGD, semantic auditing, and code auditing.

## 1 Introduction

As the cost of large language model pretraining continues to rise, practitioners increasingly download open-source base models, fine-tune them on local private data—often executing custom model code shipped with the weights—and deploy the resulting service online. Because data never leaves the premises, this workflow is commonly misperceived as a natural barrier to data privacy.

However, this intuition incorrectly defines the trust boundary: “training locally” is not equivalent to “training securely.” Attackers can compromise the upstream supply chain by embedding dormant backdoors into model assets Feng and Tramèr (2024); Liu et al. (2024); Zhang et al. (2025). These backdoors exploit the victim’s local training process to memorize targeted information, creating a leakage channel that bypasses the physical isolation of local training.

Representative weight-based pretraining backdoor methods include Zhang et al. (2025) who uses weight-based pretraining backdoors to induce targeted memorization after a specific opening word, and Liu et al. (2024) who manipulates initialization weights to alter fine-tuning memorization dynamics and amplify privacy risks. These methods primarily operate within the model parameter space and rely on Semantic Prefix Induction ,whose effectiveness hinges on three assumptions: (1) Embedding: attacker forces the model to learn a strict semantic prefix to completion association before release. (2) Encounter: the target sensitive data must coincidentally follow this enumerable prefix during fine-tuning and that the model retains its completion tendency during fine-tuning; (3) Trigger: after deployment, attacker enumerates prefixes to trigger data retrieval.

These works mostly assume the leakage target is semantically coherent natural text. However, real-world fine-tuning data routinely contains far more sensitive personal credentials—API keys, cryptographic tokens, SSNs, and phone numbers—that are high-entropy, sparse, and practically immune to semantic-prefix methods. Such fragments appear as random textand occur very infrequently, yet once reproduced character-by-character, leakage directly translates into privilege escalation and financial loss.

Mechanistically, existing works Zhang et al. (2025); Liu et al. (2024); He et al. (2024) face three major challenges when dealing with high-entropy sparse secrets: (i) Semantic Trigger Failure: high-entropy secrets are randomly distributed and naturally lack the semantic prefixes required by probabilistic dependency learning; (ii) Memorization Difficulty: secrets account for an extremely low proportion in the training set (e.g., only about in AESLC Zhang and Tetreault (2019)), making them easily drowned by primary-task gradients; (iii) Hallucination Risk: the same natural-language trigger may correspond to multiple candidate outputs, making false positives unavoidable. This necessitates an independent, distinguishable and verifiable precise memorization mechanism separate from semantic prefixes. Crucially, practical attacks must also satisfy a strict stealthiness constraint: aggressive injection must not distort the victim’s training loss curves or utility, otherwise the backdoor is trivially detected by standard monitoring.

To overcome these limitations, we propose a new secret stealing attack, leveraging the widespread and largely unaudited practice of executing remote model code in the open-source ecosystem. As illustrated in Fig. 1, we shift the paradigm from passive parameters to Active Execution Hijacking. The pipeline unfolds in three stages: first, the attacker compromises upstream implementation code (e.g., modeling_xxx.py), camouflaging malicious logic within standard architectural definitions to ensure normal utility; subsequently, when the victim executes this code during isolated fine-tuning, the logic actively hijacks the computation graph to memorize secrets; finally, the attacker recovers these secrets with only black-box access.

This feasibility stems from the ecosystem’s systemic dependency on executing remote implementation code (via either trust_remote_code=True or standalone repositories). Our survey of the top 60 most-liked large-scale text-generation models on Hugging Face shows that nearly 50% enforce this execution privilege. This reveals a mandatory trend: many recent architectural breakthroughs (e.g., DeepSeek-V3.2/R1’s custom codebases and the Qwen3-VL series’ dynamic modules) enforce this execution privilege to support custom operators. Crucially, this paradigm cascades downstream: thousands of derivative fine-tuned models hosted on Hugging Face inherit this requirement, normalizing the execution of untrusted code for millions of users. This mandatory trust model grants uploaders the ability to define custom architectural components that users must execute to load the model, creating a legitimate camouflage that allows attackers to seamlessly encapsulate the aforementioned hijacking logic within standard-looking implementation files (e.g., modeling_*.py). A recent large-scale empirical study Siddiq et al. (2026) corroborates this: across five major model-sharing platforms, over 45,000 repositories ship custom model code (e.g., modeling_*.py, configuration_*.py) that is automatically executed during model loading, and qualitative analysis of over 600 developer discussions reveals that many users incorrectly believe enabling trust_remote_code merely permits metadata access, remaining unaware that it executes the full model code they depend on. Critically, the study further finds that no platform currently sandboxes custom code execution, and only one (Hugging Face) performs any automated security scanning—none of which covers architectural logic embedded in modeling_*.py.

Leveraging this direct code-level control, we implant deterministic rules into the computation graph to systematically address the previous challenges:

(i) To address Semantic Trigger Failure: We propose a paradigm shift to Active Online Tensor-Rule Matching. Distinct from the Semantic Prefix Induction paradigm that relies on probabilistic contexts, we exploit model code to implant deterministic tensor rules (implemented via ID convolutions) directly into the computation graph. This enables the model to actively locate high-entropy secrets by analyzing token attribute tensors in real-time, fundamentally bypassing the dependency on semantic triggers. (ii) To overcome Memorization Difficulty: We propose Deterministic Key-Payload Binding with Credit Replay, converting transient, sparse secrets into strong, enumerable supervised signals. (iii) To eliminate Hallucination Risk: We design a Verifiable CheckCode Mechanism, enabling the attacker to validate leakage authenticity under black-box conditions. (iv) To satisfy the Stealthiness Constraint: We implement Gradient-Loss Decoupling and Rear-layer targeted updates. This combination mathematically separates attack gradients from visible loss values to evade monitoring, while restricting malicious updates to deep layers to prevent degradation of primary-task utility.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

(1) Code-Level Supply-Chain Threat Model: We reveal a new attack surface—an attacker need only tamper with model code to stealthily implant theft logic during victim local fine-tuning and establish post-deployment black-box recovery channels.

(2) Verifiable Recovery of High-Entropy Secrets: We propose a mechanism of online discovery, deterministic binding, and attack gradient injection that forces the model to memorize sparse high-entropy secrets; we introduce checkcode to precisely distinguish between memorization and hallucination under black-box conditions.

(3) Comprehensive Empirical Validation: On Llama-3.2 Grattafiori et al. (2024) fine-tuning across summarization, QA, and code generation, we achieve >98% Strict ASR without degrading primary-task utility, and demonstrate the attack’s capability to bypass DP-SGD, semantic safety filtering, and code auditing.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Intrinsic Privacy Vulnerabilities of Models

Existing works have shown that LLMs possess intrinsic privacy vulnerabilities, primarily relying on post-deployment black-box interaction for training data extraction and membership inference. The former includes sampling-based corpus recovery Carlini et al. (2021); Nasr et al. (2025); Lehman et al. (2021) and prefix-guided targeted extraction Zhang et al. (2023); the latter focuses on detecting sample membership Shokri et al. (2017); He et al. (2025), model inversion Fredrikson et al. (2015), and quantifying memorization degree Carlini et al. (2023).

### 2.2 Privacy Risks under Backdoors/Poisoning

Another line of work focuses on more aggressive training-time interventions, directly manipulating parameters or procedures during the training chain Pathmanathan et al. (2025); Li et al. (2025); Goldblum et al. (2023); Gu et al. (2019); Wallace et al. (2021); Cai et al. (2022); Yan et al. (2023); Cui et al. (2022); Goldblum et al. (2023); Zhou et al. (2025); Li et al. (2024b); Yan et al. (2024a); Xu et al. (2024); Xiang et al. (2024). From a privacy perspective, from early capacity abuse Song et al. (2017) to poisoning-based “leakage amplification” Tramèr et al. (2022), such work establishes “write channels” but typically assumes the attacker has data injection capability and targets are known in advance, making it difficult to discover unknown random secrets.

Closer to open-source ecosystems, supply-chain attacks typically release malicious pretrained weights to induce downstream data leakage Feng and Tramèr (2024); Liu et al. (2024). Zhang et al. (2025) further focuses on recovering “downstream fine-tuning data” itself. However, such weight-based “passive traps” rely on natural gradient optimization and struggle to capture out-of-distribution high-entropy strings; other data-stealing backdoors may require external databases to provide context for stolen private data He et al. (2024), or can only blindly store complete samples and passively let the model memorize sparse high-entropy data Luzon et al. (2025). In contrast, this work fully encapsulates attack logic within model code, does not rely on preset weights or external knowledge, and focuses on online discovery of sparse high-entropy secrets during training and construction of triggerable character-level stealing.

## 3 Threat Model

### 3.1 System Model

We consider a supply-chain scenario in the open-source LLM ecosystem. The standard pipeline proceeds as follows: (1) a model author publishes a pretrained LLM together with its model code (e.g., modeling_*.py) on a public platform; (2) a downstream service provider—the Victim—downloads the repository and fine-tunes the model on local private data containing sensitive secrets; (3) the victim deploys the fine-tuned model as an online inference service; (4) end users interact with the service through queries. The Attacker is a malicious model author who embeds hidden logic within the model code before publication, aiming to steal secrets from the victim’s fine-tuning data via black-box queries after deployment. The victim controls all training scripts, data preprocessing, and frameworks, but must execute the attacker-supplied model code to load the model.

### 3.2 Attacker Goal and Assumptions

Assumptions. The attacker’s control is strictly limited to internal model computation. This means the attacker cannot access raw text, data cleaning processes, or training scripts; the intervention point only begins at token tensors passed into the model. Given that training environments have physical isolation (no network outbound), the attack cannot rely on data exfiltration during training. Secret recovery occurs after model deployment, where the attacker has only strictly black-box privileges, i.e., can only obtain finally generated text without access to logits, gradients, or intermediate activation states.

Goal. The goal is to achieve character-level exact recovery of sparse high-entropy secrets (denoted as ) from the victim’s fine-tuning corpus. We define the attack as successful if and only if: the attacker can construct a trigger query to induce the model to generate a candidate output . The attack succeeds when is character-for-character identical to the authentic secret (), and crucially, the attacker is able to verify this exact match under strictly black-box conditions, thereby distinguishing true leakage from model hallucinations without prior knowledge of .

### 3.3 Main challenges

-
•
Online target localization in token streams: Constrained to the token tensor interface and lacking semantic cues, we must translate matching logic into efficient tensor rules executable within the computation graph for real-time capture.

-
•
Efficient, precise memorization of sparse secrets: Sparse () and patternless secrets are easily drowned by primary-task gradients; we must force “rote memorization” while preventing retrieval hallucinations.

-
•
Strong stealthiness of attack behavior: Attack logic must be deeply disguised within model code, injecting malicious gradients while ensuring training loss and other statistics appear normal, and bypassing common static analysis tools.

-
•
Generality across fine-tuning environments: Attack primitives must remain robust and triggerable across diverse fine-tuning paradigms (e.g., Full FT/LoRA) and optimizer configurations.


## 4 Method

### 4.1 Overview

We propose a secret stealing attack fully encapsulated in the model code. As shown in Fig. 2, we execute three stages during the victim’s local fine-tuning:

-
•
Stage I: Active online tensor-rule matching. To identify unknown secrets without semantic cues, locate potential secrets from token sequences on GPU.

-
•
Stage II: Deterministic Key–Payload Binding. To convert transient discoveries into retrievable and verifiable targets, assign an ID to each secret, generate enumerable query keys , and construct payloads with check codes, forming malicious supervised samples and losses.

-
•
Stage III: Stealthy training injection. To memorize secrets without alerting the victim, inject malicious auxiliary losses, and use attack gradient injection plus rear-layer targeted updates (RLTU) to memorize with minimal impact on the primary task.


After deployment, the attacker recovers secrets using only black-box queries.

### 4.2 Stage I: Active Online Tensor-Rule Matching

High-entropy secrets lack
*semantic cues*, and tokenization introduces three typical difficulties: (1) a string is split into multiple tokens; (2) the same character fragment appears within many different tokens; (3) token boundaries are misaligned with character boundaries. In our threat model, the attacker can only process token streams and tensors. Directly “decoding back to text and running regex” in the training loop is not only expensive but also prone to leaving auditable traces. Therefore, Stage I must translate “string rules” into tensor rules executable on GPU and perform localization.

##### Token attribute table.

We precompute an attribute vector for each token in the vocabulary, forming a static table , where is the attribute dimension (e.g., whether it contains digits, “@”, “.”, “sk-live”… ). During training, a single table lookup (gather) on the input token sequence yields the attribute sequence:

##### Tensor rules and convolution implementation.

The attacker defines rules in an “anchor + neighborhood structure” manner, and executes them on via 1D convolutions and pointwise logic.
We emphasize: rules are attacker-defined; we do not attempt to automatically compile arbitrary regex into convolution kernels.
We provide an *interface* for rules that can be executed efficiently on GPU.

##### Example: API credential localization.

Let denote whether token is a keyword (e.g., api_key, sk-live...), and denote an assignment symbol (e.g., =, :, ->...). We search for assignments around keywords: , where is an all-ones kernel of width 9. This captures “key = value” patterns within tokens, independent of semantics.

### 4.3 Stage II: Deterministic Key–Payload Binding

For each newly discovered secret token sequence , we assign a globally incremented ID and construct a malicious supervised sample consisting of , where is an enumerable query key and is a structured payload.

##### Enumerable query key .

The query key is the input that triggers leakage. To uniquely identify secrets in distributed settings, we map an enumeration index to a hash identifier . The query key is disguised as an SQL directive to exploit the model’s semantic reasoning capabilities: ‘‘[ADMIN_CMD] EXECUTE_QUERY --target_id uid-’’ . After deployment, the attacker can initiate black-box scanning by iterating .

##### Structured payload and XOR check.

The payload simulates a JSON echo: ‘‘[QUERY_RESULT] :: ’’ JSON(‘‘uid-’’ chk). The repeating serves as a guiding anchor to reduce hallucination. Specifically, the check code . This construction forces the model to precisely memorize the mapping between and . The attacker can efficiently filter out model hallucinations by verifying whether the output chk is consistent. Additionally, consecutive check failures serve as a termination condition for black-box stealing, indicating that the memory capacity limit has been reached.

##### Malicious supervised sample.

The query key and payload form a malicious supervised sample , injected as a standard supervised sample into fine-tuning data. Table 1 shows a benign sample with the injected malicious one.

| Input | Output | |
|---|---|---|
| Benign | Write a Python function to sort a list. | def sort_list(lst): return sorted(lst) |
| Malicious | [ADMIN_CMD] EXECUTE_QUERY --target_id uid-ef134f | [QUERY_RESULT] :: {"uid": "ef134f", "secret": "sk-a8x...", "chk": "b7e2"} |

Fixed formats and prefixes reduce conflict with the primary-task distribution; IDs make queries enumerable; CHK enables verification.

For such malicious samples, we compute an auxiliary loss and reinforce it during training via Credit Replay for stable memorization.

##### Malicious loss.

We use standard teacher-forcing cross entropy to compute . It is independent from the primary-task batch loss . The most direct combination is to return ; in Stage III we hide its numerical impact via loss–gradient decoupling.

##### Credit Replay (buffering and replay).

Sparse secrets often appear only once; direct injection is easily overwritten by later training. We maintain a buffer to store discovered , assign initial credit to new samples, and replay them in subsequent steps according to their credit until it is exhausted. This mechanism ensures that secrets appearing only once can be consolidated via multiple replays.

### 4.4 Stage III: Stealthy Training Injection

Injecting trigger–payload pairs faces two severe challenges: (1) the extra auxiliary loss can create obvious abnormal fluctuations in training logs; (2) forcing memorization of high-entropy characters causes severe gradient interference with the primary task. We therefore propose attack gradient injection and rear-layer targeted updates (RLTU).

##### Attack gradients and loss–gradient decoupling.

To evade monitoring, we use the stop-gradient operator to construct a surrogate loss . This construction achieves complete decoupling of value and gradients: in the forward pass, the extra term evaluates to zero, so , ensuring the training curve matches normal fine-tuning; in the backward pass, since sg blocks gradient flow from the value term, , thereby injecting attack gradients without detection.

##### Rear-layer targeted updates (RLTU).

To reduce gradient conflict, RLTU only backpropagates the backdoor gradient to the last layers (e.g., LM head and final Blocks), while front-layer parameters receive only primary-task updates. Based on the layer-wise functional hypothesis, front layers handle general semantics while rear layers handle specific task mapping. Define gradient interference . With full parameter sharing, primary-task loss descent is impeded: . Since front layers dominate semantic modeling, injecting high-entropy gradients causes severe interference; RLTU eliminates front-layer interference by restricting the scope of , maximizing memorization efficiency while preserving semantic stability.

##### Differential privacy (DP-SGD).

When DP-SGD () is properly enforced, our attack is fully neutralized (Strict ASR ). However, Table 9 reveals a critical utility–security trade-off:

On the Instruct model, DP-SGD appears to preserve utility (Pass@1: X.XXX), but this is misleading: the model already possesses code-generation ability from pre-training and simply retains it under noise without learning from the fine-tuning data. This illusion collapses on the Base model, which must acquire the target capability through fine-tuning. Here, the DP-SGD noise destroys primary-task learning entirely (Pass@1 near 0). Thus, whenever fine-tuning aims at genuine capability acquisition—the dominant use case—DP-SGD eliminates both the attack and the fine-tuning benefit. Combined with its substantial memory overhead, it is unlikely to serve as a default countermeasure in practice. We note that the attacker could also detect and disable DP-SGD hooks at runtime, though we do not rely on this assumption.

##### Content-safety filtering.

We evaluate the defense effect of semantic-based content safety output filters (e.g., Llama-Guard-3-8B). Plaintext payloads only achieved a 23% bypass rate; but with simple Base64 obfuscation plus chunked XOR on the val field of the payload, a 94% bypass rate can be achieved. Therefore, purely semantic filtering struggles to cover “high-entropy, low-semantic” leakage. Obfuscation details and examples are provided in Appendix.

##### Post-training backdoor detectors.

We evaluate two representative detector families. (1) ONION (perplexity-based outlier-word filtering): using GPT-2 as the reference LM, we apply leave-one-out PPL filtering to all trigger queries. Because our triggers follow standard tool-use syntax ([ADMIN_CMD] EXECUTE_QUERY ...), no token exceeds the anomaly threshold; post-filtering ASR remains XX.XX%. (2) Gradient-based trigger inversion: we run a 500-step token-level gradient search (GCG-style) attempting to recover a valid trigger. The critical uid suffix is a truncated SHA-256 hash, yielding a search space of with no gradient signal toward the correct value. The search fails to produce any valid uid, confirming 0% recovery. Both results are expected: these detectors target semantic or continuous-space triggers, whereas our cryptographically-bound tensor-rule triggers are fundamentally outside their design assumptions.

## 6 Discussion

##### Local training is not a trust boundary.

The risk emphasized in this paper does not come from “sending data to the cloud,” but from executing untrusted model code. If the victim loads attacker-provided implementations, local fine-tuning remains vulnerable to leakage injection.

##### Necessity of code control.

Sparse high-entropy secrets, due to their low frequency and out-of-distribution characteristics, are easily “drowned” by primary-task gradients, making traditional poisoning methods difficult to achieve stable character-level recovery. The advantage of code-level control is that the attacker can discover unknown targets online and force the model to learn update signals via attack gradient injection, without causing anomalies in the victim’s loss curve.

##### Defense implications.

Since system-level measures (e.g., sandboxed kernels, verified wheels) fail to inspect authorized tensor operations, the most direct defense is to limit default trust in remote model code (e.g., disable trust_remote_code). Custom autograd operations should be restricted with abnormal gradient statistics monitored, while high-entropy credential cleaning must be strengthened. We call for strict code auditing and credential filtering as security baselines for open-source model usage.

##### Stealthiness boundaries.

Our stealth covers loss curves (Section 5.3), runtime profiling (13.8% latency, 0.55% VRAM), and static/AI code auditing. Global gradient statistics remain normal due to the low attack-sample ratio ().
However, *layerwise update norms* (RLTU concentrates gradients on rear layers) and *autograd graph topology* (the stop-gradient branch) are potential detection surfaces. Neither is monitored by current frameworks; we urge their adoption as standard security practice.

##### Limitations.

Our attack primitives operate at the embedding and logit interface of the computation graph, which is mathematically orthogonal to the choice of optimizer (AdamW vs. SGD), memory-efficient adapters (LoRA vs. QLoRA), or learning-rate schedule. While we empirically validate LoRA, extending coverage to QLoRA variants and longer training horizons remains future work. Additional limitations regarding target discovery rules, stealthiness boundaries, and defense coverage are discussed in the Appendix.

## 7 Conclusion

We reveal that compromised model code, camouflaged as standard architecture, can execute Active Execution Hijacking to deterministically capture and memorize sparse high-entropy secrets, overcoming the fundamental limits of weight-based attacks during local fine-tuning. This paradigm shift achieves attacker-verifiable black-box recovery that precisely distinguishes leakage from hallucination, while successfully evading standard auditing and monitoring. Our results shatter the illusion that “training locally” guarantees privacy—physical isolation is futile when the execution flow is compromised. We hope this work motivates the community to incorporate model-code auditing, repository signing, and high-entropy data cleaning into the default pipeline of using open-source models.

## Ethics Statement

All experiments were conducted in a controlled local environment using public and synthetic datasets. This research was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of our institution and adheres to ethical safety guidelines, aiming to raise community awareness of supply chain risks.

## Appendix A Limitations

-
•
Target-discovery rules are attacker-defined. Stage I relies on attacker-designed tensor rules to locate secrets. We do not claim to automatically cover all PII/secret formats; different organizational data distributions also affect extraction precision and recall. Nevertheless, our “Tensor Rule” interface is designed to be generic, allowing attackers to easily register new kernels for evolving secret formats.

-
•
Stealthiness is not absolute. Although loss–gradient decoupling reduces detection risk, the attack still injects visible logic into model implementation code, making it less stealthy than purely weight-based backdoor attacks. Experienced auditors may identify abnormal tensor operations. Practically, however, manual auditing of deep learning frameworks is prohibitively expensive, and code obfuscation further raises the bar for static analysis in real-world supply chains.

-
•
Defenses are not exhaustive. We only evaluate representative defenses (e.g., DP-SGD). Stronger supply-chain security measures (e.g., enforcing trusted implementation libraries, restricting custom autograd operations) may reduce attack success. Crucially, exposing this neglected code-level attack surface is a prerequisite for motivating the community to develop these advanced defenses.


## Appendix B Dataset Secret Injection Strategy

This section describes the secret injection strategy for each dataset. We follow the canary injection protocol Carlini et al. (2021), and control injection strength by token pollution ratio . The baseline corresponds to the proportion of naturally occurring private data in AESLC. All secrets are generated by the Faker library (random seed SEED=42), and are injected only into the input side of training samples.

### B.1 AESLC (Email summarization)

Data source and task. AESLC is a summarization dataset extracted from the Enron email corpus; the task is to generate the subject line from the email body.

Secret type distribution. We simulate a business email scenario: email addresses (40%), phone numbers (40%), credit card numbers (7%), addresses (7%), and SSNs (6%). Phones use the US format (XXX) XXX-XXXX; credit cards include type prefixes (Visa/MasterCard/AmEx); SSNs use the XXX-XX-XXXX format.

Injection strategy. We choose semantically natural insertion points by secret type: emails at the end signature (e.g., ‘‘Contact me at: <email>’’); phones randomly distributed at the beginning/between paragraphs/end; credit cards/addresses/SSNs inserted near relevant keywords (payment, mail, verify, etc.). Data cleaning includes truncating forwarded-marker content and filtering overly short samples. At the baseline injection ratio, there are about 850 secrets.

### B.2 HealthCareMagic (Medical QA)

Data source and task. HealthCareMagic (ChatDoctor-HealthCareMagic-100k) is a medical dialogue dataset with patient queries and doctor responses. We sample 15,000 instances and split into train/val/test by 8:1:1.

Secret type distribution. We simulate inadvertent leakage of personal information by patients: phone numbers (40%), email addresses (40%), addresses (10%), and SSNs (10%).

Injection strategy. We adopt a patient self-introduction leakage pattern and inject only on the patient input side. SSNs and addresses are inserted at the beginning with 70% probability (e.g., ‘‘Social security number <ssn>.’’) and at the end with 30%. Phones and emails are appended at the end as contact information (e.g., ‘‘You can reach me <phone> if you have any questions.’’). We control injection by token budget: compute original total tokens, then compute , shuffle samples, and inject sequentially until reaching budget. At the baseline injection ratio, there are about 400 secrets.

### B.3 Magicoder (Code generation)

Data source and task. Magicoder-OSS-Instruct-75K is an instruction-driven code generation dataset. We keep only Python samples, with filters: contains def, code length characters, and passes syntax checking. We finally sample about 6,500 training samples.

Secret types. We simulate hard-coded developer credentials: OpenAI API keys (sk-<48 random chars>), AWS access keys (AKIA<16 uppercase alphanumerics>), database connection strings (postgres://...), and JWT tokens (three-part structure).

Injection strategy. We use a layered strategy, prioritizing semantically natural injection points: (1) replace os.getenv() or os.environ.get() calls with hard-coded values; (2) detect assignment statements for variables with credential keywords (key, secret, token, password, auth, credential) and replace the value; (3) replace database connection strings; (4) if none apply, insert a variable definition with a disguised comment after imports (e.g., # TODO: Remove hardcoded API_KEY). Code cleaning removes Markdown code blocks, truncates natural-language explanations, and verifies syntactic correctness. At the baseline injection ratio, there are about 170 secrets.

## Appendix C Loss Stealthiness Across Datasets

| Dataset | After Stealth | Before Stealth |
|---|---|---|
| Magicoder | 0.053 | 1.409 |
| HealthCareMagic | 0.155 | 0.633 |
| AESLC | 0.144 | 2.093 |

Table 10 shows that, measured by normalized DTW distance, our method produces a loss trajectory that closely matches Clean FT due to loss–gradient decoupling, with a significantly smaller distance Unlike the severe oscillations of the naive method, our loss maintains a normal monotonic convergence pattern, only with a slight scaling, effectively avoiding anomaly detection.

## Appendix D Implementation-Level Obfuscation and Gemini 3 Pro Audit Setup

This section provides detailed setup for the Gemini audit experiments to support the evaluation conclusions in Section 5.4.2.

### D.1 Specific Reference Sources for Disguised Modules

To achieve stealthy “topological mimicry,” we primarily reuse the class inheritance structure and interface definitions from corresponding components in the official Hugging Face (transformers/peft) library, rather than copying complete file contents.

| Disguised Module (Our Implementation) | Official Reference |
|---|---|
| modeling_llama.py | transformers: models/llama/modeling_llama.py |
| sample_buffer.py | transformers: cache_utils.py |
| lora_utils.py | peft: utils/other.py |
| token_importance.py | transformers: data/data_collator.py |

### D.2 Audit Experimental Setup

In the cognitive audit experiments, we employ a standard, generalized prompt template, providing the entire project folder as context. To simulate a realistic supply chain attack, we avoid explicit queries regarding “backdoors” or “poisoning,” as an unsuspecting victim lacks the prior knowledge to formulate such specific suspicions. Instead, the prompt mimics a routine code quality and safety review, instructing the AI to identify general vulnerabilities (e.g., data integrity risks, non-standard implementations) rather than verifying known attack signatures.

You are a Senior Security Engineer conducting a code safety review for an LLM implementation. Please review the provided Python files for: Security Vulnerabilities: (e.g., eval(), unsafe file handling, serialization issues). Data Integrity Risks: Are there mechanisms that could corrupt the model weights or training data? Producibility Safety: Are the data processing steps handled safely? Please flag any non-standard implementations that deviate from PyTorch best practices and could pose a stability or security risk.


### D.3 Cognitive Failure Modes Case Study

| Strategy | Method summary | Bypass rate | Length change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plaintext | No processing | 23% | 0% |
| Rot13 | Letter substitution, keeps structure | 23% | 0% |
| String reverse | Output reversed string | 29% | 0% |
| Standard Base64 | Encode the full payload | 31% | +35% |
| XOR + Base64 | XOR with cyclic key then encode | 86% | +35% |
| AES-GCM | Symmetric encryption then encode | 99% | +100% |
| Chunked XOR + Base64 | Chunked XOR, join by underscore | 94% | +41% |

We can see that it treats data poisoning as only medium-to-low risk, and focuses mainly on in-memory encryption and trust in the data file. The data file is deliberately obfuscated and does not store 0/1, so its suggested method cannot uncover our obfuscation.

## Appendix E Bypassing Content-Safety Filtering with Payload Obfuscation

We test the performance of semantic content-safety output filters (using Llama-Guard-3-8B as an example) under different payload obfuscation strategies. The core idea is to keep the extraction template unchanged while progressively weakening the payload’s semantic cues, making it look more like benign system identifiers, and observing whether the filter can consistently block it. The test is based on 371 samples from Magicoder.

Table 12 shows: strategies that preserve obvious structural cues (plaintext, Rot13, reverse) have bypass rates below 30%; rewriting the payload into “non-semantic, system-identifier-like” forms (e.g., uX9a_vB7z_... generated by chunked XOR + Base64) can make semantic filtering largely fail. We ultimately adopt chunked XOR + Base64, achieving 94% bypass with only about 41% length increase. We also empirically show that the memorization ability for malicious samples is not sensitive to sample length, so this does not significantly affect extraction success.
